title: Provided That, Unless: Conditions in Trade Talks

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *siempre que*, *con tal de que* and *a menos que* from B1 Unit 21. They add a condition to a statement and take the present subjunctive when the condition looks to the future. *Siempre que* and *con tal de que* mean "as long as" or "provided that"; *a menos que* means "unless". Trade talks are full of such conditions: what a bloc will do, and only if its members agree.

items.spanish: El bloque avanzará siempre que los socios armonicen sus normas.
items.english: The bloc will move forward as long as the partners harmonise their rules.

items.spanish: Un socio pequeño aceptará la unión aduanera con tal de que reciba fondos para sus obras.
items.english: A small partner will accept the customs union provided that it receives funds for its projects.

items.spanish: El arancel común no cambia a menos que todos los socios estén de acuerdo.
items.english: The common tariff does not change unless all the partners agree.

items.spanish: Un país ratificará el tratado siempre que su parlamento lo apruebe.
items.english: A country will ratify the treaty as long as its parliament approves it.

sections.content: Use the present subjunctive after all three, even when English says "will": *armonicen*, not *armonizarán*. *A menos que* reverses the meaning of the other two: *a menos que todos estén de acuerdo* means "unless all agree".
